'''''Polytrichum strictum''''', commonly known as '''bog haircap moss'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://eol.org/pages/923292/overview|title=''Polytrichum strictum'' - Polytrichum strictum - Overview - Encyclopedia of Life|website=Encyclopedia of Life|language=en|access-date=2017-05-07}}</ref> or '''strict haircap''',<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Mosses and Liverworts of Britain and Ireland - A Field Guide|last=Atherton, I., Bosanquet, S.,& Lawley, M.|publisher=British Bryological Society|year=2010|isbn=9780956131010|location=Plymouth, UK|pages=326}}</ref> is an [[evergreen]] and [[perennial]] species of [[moss]] native to ''[[Sphagnum]]'' [[bog]]s and other moist habitats in temperate climates.  It has a [[Circumboreal Region|circumboreal]] distribution, and is also found in [[South America]] and [[Antarctica]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065140|title=Polytrichum strictum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2017-05-07}}</ref>

== Description ==
Like other species in the [[Polytrichaceae]], ''Polytrichum strictum'' has leaves with a single costa, vertical [[Lamella (surface anatomy)|lamellae]], a water-repelling [[cuticle]], and [[rhizoid]]s that appear to facilitate external water movement in addition to anchoring the plant.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www.bryoecol.mtu.edu/|title=Bryophyte Ecology, Volume 1: Physical Ecology|last=Glime|first=Janice|date=2007|website=Bryophyte Ecology|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref>  Dense tufts of slender stems from 6–12 cm form 20–40 cm hummocks in [[bog]]s and similar substrates.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />  Leaves are narrowly lanceolate, appressed to the stem when dry and spreading to erect when moist.<ref name=":2" /> The reddish awn (formed by the slightly excurrent costa) and smooth, inrolled leaf margins separate ''P. strictum'' from other [[Polytrichum]] species; only [[Polytrichum juniperinum|juniper haircap moss (''P. juniperinum)'']] shares these attributes.<ref name=":1" /> ''P. strictum'', however, can be easily distinguished by the wooly-tomentose white rhizoids that extend up its stems (absent in ''[[Polytrichum juniperinum|P. juniperinum]]''), as well as its boggy habitat and predilection for organic soils (in contrast to the weedy nature and preference for mineral soils that characterize ''[[Polytrichum juniperinum|P. juniperinum]]'').<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Plants of Coastal British Columbia|last=Pojar, J., & Mackinnon, A.|publisher=Lone Pine|year=2004|isbn=1551055325|location=Vancouver, BC|pages=452}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Polytrichum strictum'' is found throughout [[Canada]], the northern half of the [[United States]], Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands, northern Europe and Asia, as well as Antarctica and the southern half of South America.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />  It is characteristic of boggy peatland habitats dominated by ''[[Sphagnum]]'' mosses, but can also be found in wet [[heath]]s, [[tundra]], [[Cyperaceae|sedge]] meadows, and peaty forests from low to high elevations; in warmer climates, it is largely confined to relict [[bog]]s.<ref name=":2" />  Its microhabitat is at the top of peat hummocks, which it often helps to form.<ref name=":2" />

== Reproduction ==
[[File:Polytrichum strictum maennchen.jpeg|thumb|The male reproductive structures of ''P. strictum,'' featuring splash cups.]]
[[File:Polytrichum strictum sporogonen.jpeg|thumb|Immature [[sporophyte]]s of ''P. strictum,'' with calyptra clearly visible.]]
''Polytrichum strictum'' is [[dioicous]],<ref name=":2" /> with male and female reproductive structures produced separately by male and female [[gametophytes]], which are [[haploid]] (1n).  As in other ''[[Polytrichum]]'' species, the [[Antheridium|antheridia]] are borne terminally on male plants and swell and burst when mature, launching [[sperm]] into the air; in addition, they develop in splash cups, which further facilitate sperm dispersal by catching and harnessing the energy of rain drops.<ref name=":3" />  The lucky few sperm to land near the [[archegonia]] of a female plant (also borne terminally) use their two whiplash [[Flagellum|flagella]] to swim down the neck and into the venter, where one will fertilize the [[Egg cell|ovum]]. Once [[fertilisation]] takes place, the [[zygote]] develops into the [[diploid]] (2n) [[sporophyte]], which consists of a foot (embedded in the tissue of the gametophyte), a seta (or stalk), and a capsule.<ref name=":3" />  The capsule, which is covered by a dirty-white [[calyptra]], matures after the seta elongates, at which point the calyptra is shed.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />   Within the capsule, each sporoctye undergoes [[meiosis]] to produce four haploid (1n) [[spore]]s; when these are mature, the [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] is projected and the spores are released through the [[peristome]], which is joined by the [[epiphragm]] and ringed by 64 nematodontous teeth.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />  When the proper conditions and substrate are available, the spores [[Germination|germinate]] into a filamentous [[protonema]], from which the gametophytes emerge, completing the cycle.

== Use in restoration ==
[[File:Polytrichum strictum (a, 150144-481741) 8634.JPG|thumb|''P. strictum'' leaf cross section, showing lamellae, costa, and inrolled leaf margin]]
''Polytrichum strictum'' is considered an important [[pioneer species]] in peatlands, able to tolerate a wide range of environmental conditions and disturbance regimes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nait.ca/docs/Peatland_Site_Revegetation.pdf|title=Peatland Site Revegetation|last=Sobze, J.M., Gauthier, M.E., Xu, B., & Schoonmaker, A.|date=November 2013|website=Boreal Research Institute|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref>  It is instrumental in preventing [[frost heaving]] in harvested peatlands, and research suggests it can be used in the restoration of unstable peat areas, although little is known about whether it aids or hinders ''Sphagnum'' growth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Groeneveld, E.V.G., & Rochefort, L.|date=March 2005|title=Polytrichum strictum as a Solution to Frost Heaving in Disturbed Ecosystems: A Case Study with Milled Peatlands|url=http://www.gret-perg.ulaval.ca/uploads/tx_centrerecherche/Groeneveld_Rest_Ecol_2005_02.pdf|journal=Restoration Ecology|volume=13|issue=1|pages=74–82|doi=10.1111/j.1526-100x.2005.00009.x|bibcode=2005ResEc..13...74G|s2cid=56332150}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
